question: Is random search a more efficient strategy than grid search (and manual search) for hyper-parameter optimization of neural networks and deep belief networks?
hypothesis: Random search is more efficient than grid search in high-dimensional spaces because the response function Psi has low effective dimensionality.
contributions: Empirical comparison of random search vs grid search on neural networks (Larochelle et al. 2007 setup)
Gaussian process / ARD analysis showing low effective dimensionality of Psi that differs by dataset
Simulation comparing grid, random, Sobol, Niederreiter, Halton and latin hypercube point sets
Comparison with expert manual+grid search on 32-dimensional DBN configuration
Procedure for estimating generalization of best model under uncertainty about which trial is best, and the random experiment efficiency curve

method.summary: Random search (i.i.d. uniform draws, log-uniform for scale parameters) over the same configuration space as the grid of Larochelle et al. 2007. 256 trials per dataset are subsampled into experiments of size 1 to 32 or 64 to give efficiency curves, compared with the published grid-search accuracy (average 100 trials) for NNs and grid-assisted manual search (average 41 trials) for DBNs. A GP with ARD squared-exponential kernels is fit to validation performance to estimate per-hyper-parameter relevance.
method.task: Hyper-parameter optimization; image classification on MNIST variants, rectangles, convex

datasets.name: mnist background images
datasets.source: MNIST digit composited (max) on natural image patch

datasets.name: mnist rotated background images
datasets.source: rotated MNIST on natural image patch

datasets.name: rectangles
datasets.source: synthetic 28x28 rectangle outlines, tall vs wide (2 classes)

datasets.name: rectangles images
datasets.source: synthetic, rectangles filled with natural image patch

datasets.name: convex
datasets.source: synthetic 28x28 binary images, convex vs non-convex

models.name: single-layer neural network
models.architecture: 1 hidden layer, sigmoid or tanh, zero-initialised output weights

models.name: Deep Belief Network (1, 2 or 3 layers)
models.architecture: stacked RBMs pretrained by contrastive divergence then fine-tuned; 8 global + 8 per-layer hyper-parameters = 32 for 3 layers

training.objective: classification error (zero-one loss), mean over minibatches
training.lr: NN: initial learning rate drawn geometrically 0.001 to 10.0; DBN finetune log-uniform 0.001 to 10; CD lr log-uniform 0.0001 to 1.0
training.lr_schedule: eps_t = t0*eps0 / max(t,t0), t0 drawn geometrically 300 to 30000 (NN); DBN anneal start log-uniform 100 to 10000 (finetune), 10 to 10000 (CD)
training.epochs: min 100, max 1000 iterations over training data; stop if best validation was before iteration t/2
training.weight_decay: l2 penalty applied with 50% probability, strength drawn exponentially 3.1e-7 to 3.1e-5 (NN); DBN: 0 w.p. 0.5 else log-uniform 1e-7 to 1e-4
training.compute: 256 trials per dataset per search space (NN)
training.seeds: NN weights: one of 3 Mersenne Twister seeds; DBN: seed one of 2, 3, 4

other.nn_hyperparameters_7: activation (sigmoid/tanh), n hidden units, initial W algo, initial W norm, weight penalty, learning rate, learning-rate annealing
other.nn_hyperparameters_9: adds preprocessing type (none, normalize, PCA) and PCA variance kept uniform 0.5 to 1.0
other.init: distribution uniform(-1,1) or unit normal; scale heuristic (a) multiplier uniform (0.2,2.0) / sqrt(inputs) or (b) sqrt(6)/sqrt(inputs+hidden)

inference.samples: 256 i.i.d. trials per dataset; experiments of size s formed as N=S/s independent sub-experiments (e.g. 32 experiments of 8); DBN figure uses up to 128 trials

parameters.gp: squared exponential kernel per hyper-parameter multiplied; length scales by marginal likelihood; 50 refits on random 80% subsets, length scale init uniform 0.1 to 2; hyper-parameters rescaled to unit interval, log scale for geometric/exponential ones
parameters.qmc_simulation: 100 random target problems; target 1% of unit hypercube; 3-d and 5-d, cube or hyper-rectangle; experiments up to 512 trials; Sobol used to represent Sobol/Halton/Niederreiter

metrics.name: test accuracy of best model by validation
metrics.definition: Gaussian-mixture weighted mean of test scores, each trial weighted by probability of being best on validation (Eq 5, 6; weights by simulation, a few tens of draws)

baselines: grid search NN, average 100 trials (Larochelle et al. 2007)
manual+grid search DBN-1 and DBN-3, average 41 trials for DBN-3 (Larochelle et al. 2007)
grid, Sobol, latin hypercube in simulation
eval.protocol: Efficiency curves from subsampling 256 i.i.d. trials; GP relevance via 50 refits; no seeds/significance test beyond the 95% interval from Eq 6

evidence.quote: We formed experiments for each data set by drawing S = 256 trials from this distribution.

results.claim: Across the 8 datasets, the 7-hyper-parameter NN response surface has effective dimension between 1 and 4, depending on the dataset (ARD length scales)
results.setup: GP-ARD on the 7-hyper-parameter raw-preprocessing NN, Fig 7
results.quote: Even in this simple 7-d problem, Ψ has a much lower effective dimension of between 1 and 4,
results.note: Dimension 1 or 2 for mnist basic, mnist background images, mnist background random, rectangles images; 3 or 4 for convex, mnist rotated, rectangles.

results.claim: The learning rate is always among the important hyper-parameters; others vary by dataset
results.quote: The learning rate is always important, but sometimes the learning rate annealing rate was important (rectangles

results.claim: Random search with 8 trials matches or outperforms grid search averaging 100 trials (NN, no preprocessing)
results.setup: Single-hidden-layer neural network, 7 hyper-parameters (no preprocessing), 8 classification datasets from Larochelle et al. 2007 (MNIST variants, rectangles, convex), S=256 random trials per dataset; grid accuracy taken from Larochelle et al. 2007, dashed line
results.quote: Random searches of 8 trials match or outperform grid searches of (on average) 100 trials.
results.note: Text p.291 states it for the 71/256 trials with no preprocessing. Exact accuracy values are only in the figure, not in text.

results.claim: In the larger 9-hyper-parameter space (adds normalise/PCA preprocessing), 32 trials were needed to consistently beat the grid instead of 8
results.setup: Single-hidden-layer neural network, 9 hyper-parameters incl. preprocessing, 8 classification datasets from Larochelle et al. 2007 (MNIST variants, rectangles, convex), S=256 random trials per dataset
results.quote: In the larger space, 32 trials were necessary to consistently outperform grid search rather than 8,

results.claim: With 64 or more trials, the larger space finds better models than the restricted one
results.setup: 9-hyper-parameter NN space, grid average 100 trials without preprocessing
results.quote: with random search 64 trials are enough to ﬁnd better models in a larger less promising space

results.claim: Grid over just four PCA variance levels would have needed 5x as many trials (average 500)
results.setup: grid extension of the Larochelle et al. grid
results.quote: Exploring just four PCA variance levels by grid search would have required 5 times as many (average 500) trials

results.claim: Nine-trial illustration: a 3x3 grid tests the important parameter at only 3 distinct values; 9 random trials test 9 distinct values
results.unit: distinct values of the important parameter
results.setup: f(x,y)=g(x)+h(y)≈g(x), one important and one unimportant parameter; the figure draws 9 trials
results.quote: With grid search, nine trials only test g(x) in three distinct places. With random search, all nine trials explore distinct values of g.

results.claim: A grid with 4 values on each of the few important axes would need 256 trials, versus 8 to 16 random trials
results.setup: 4 important axes x 4 values = 256 (4^4); NN 7-d problem
results.quote: a grid with, say, four values in each of these axes would already require 256 trials,

results.claim: Random search on 32-dim DBN: better than manual+grid on 1 dataset, equal on 4, worse on 3 (128 random trials vs average 41 grid-assisted trials)
results.quote: random search found a better model than the manual search in one data set (convex), an equally good model in four (mnist basic, mnist rotated, rectangles, and rectangles images), and an inferior model in three
results.note: Abstract says 'statistically equal performance on four of seven data sets, and superior performance on one of seven' while Section 5 and Fig 9 count eight datasets (1+4+3).

results.claim: Average number of trials for the manual+grid DBN-3 search was 41; range 13 to 102
results.setup: Larochelle et al. 2007 procedure; mnist background images 102 trials, mnist background random 13
results.quote: of trials across data sets for the DBN-3 model was 41.

results.claim: Quasi-random simulation: latin hypercube no better than random search; grids worst on axis-elongated targets
results.setup: 1% volume target, 3-d and 5-d; random search probability 1-0.99^T
results.quote: Latin hypercubes, commonly used to initialize experiments in Bayesian optimization, were no more efﬁcient than the expected performance of random search.

limits: Random search was not as good as expert sequential manual+grid search on the 32-dimensional DBN problem
All strategies studied are non-adaptive; adaptive/sequential (Bayesian) optimization left to future work
Compared to published grid results of Larochelle et al. 2007, not re-run; their scores used a different averaging technique, and the paper's averaging is slightly biased toward underestimation
Grid-side experiments were not independent across datasets (later ones benefited from earlier experience)
Only shallow NNs and DBNs on small image datasets (1000 to 10 000 train examples); no modern deep nets
Exact accuracies appear only in figures, not tables
Low effective dimension is estimated with a GP-ARD fit with non-convex length-scale optimisation (50 restarts)

terms.definition: Psi is more sensitive to changes in some dimensions than others; f(x1,x2)≈g(x1) has low effective dimension
test accuracy of best trial(s) vs experiment size, obtained by treating S i.i.d. trials as N experiments of s trials
drawing uniformly in the log domain between log(A) and log(B), exponentiating, and rounding to the nearest integer
